EasyRider: Mitigating Power Transients in Datacenter-Scale Training Workloads

Dillon Jensen email: dillonj0@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA , Obi Nnorom Jr email: obdk@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA , Grant Wilkins email: gfw@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA , Hugo Budd email: hugobudd@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA , Ram Rajagopal email: ramr@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA , Juan Rivas-Davila email: jmrivas@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA and Phil Levis email: pal@cs.stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA
© none
Abstract.

Large-scale AI model training workloads use thousands of GPUs operating in tightly synchronized loops. During synchronous communication, start-up, shut-down, and checkpointing, GPU power consumption can swing from peak to idle within milliseconds. These large and rapid load swings endanger grid infrastructure as they induce steep power ramp rates, voltage and frequency shifts, and reactive power transients that can damage transformers, converters, and protection equipment.

To solve this problem, we introduce EasyRider, a power architecture to mitigate power fluctuations at the rack level. EasyRider  uses passive components and actively-controlled auxiliary energy storage to attenuate rack power swings. A software system continually monitors the energy storage system to maximize its lifetime in the presence of frequent charge/discharge cycles. EasyRider filters rack power variations to be within grid safety requirements without requiring software modifications to AI training frameworks or wasting energy. We evaluate EasyRider on a 400​VD​C400V_{DC}-rated prototype system against published workload traces and our own GPU testbed, demonstrating its effectiveness across heterogeneous power levels and workload power profiles.

1. Introduction

Pre-training foundation models such as OpenAI’s GPT series, Anthropic’s Claude, or Google’s Gemini require tens or hundreds of thousands of GPUs/TPUs. During training, these accelerators execute synchronous compute-communicate iterations: in near lockstep, they all compute, pause to communicate, then compute again (Li and Li, 2025; Li et al., 2024). During communication events, the power draw of all of the accelerators swings from maximum power to idle within milliseconds; for an NVIDIA H100, for example, this is a 700W to 140W swing, a near-instantaneous 80% power reduction, as shown in Figure 1 (Ontiveros et al., 2025; Choukse et al., 2025). At the scale of modern training jobs in datacenters, these swings create a major problem. A modern training job that uses 50,000 GPUs (e.g. Meta’s Llama-3 (Meta, Inc., 2024)) draws 35MW when computing and drops to 7MW during communication.

The fundamental challenge with such swings is that the stability of the power grid requires a constant balance between supply and demand. To match supply to demand, the grid relies on generators that adjust output in response to load changes. Generators, however, are mechanical systems with spinning turbines, inertia, and angular momentum — properties that fundamentally limit how quickly they can adjust their output. Depending on the generator, ramping times can range from a few seconds to several hours, and bringing new generators online can take minutes to days (Gonzalez-Salazar et al., 2018; Wang and Shahidehpour, 1993). When power demand changes faster than generators can respond, the grid’s frequency and voltage move outside their narrow safe ranges, damaging the generators and other connected equipment (Kirby, 2003).

Because such damage could be catastrophic, taking service offline for weeks or longer, the grid protects itself from damage by automatically disconnecting unstable loads (Watson, 2025). However, when those loads are multi-gigawatt datacenters, the sudden loss of demand is itself a destabilizing event. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has identified that simultaneous disconnection of 2.0–2.6 GW of datacenter load could destabilize the entire Texas grid and trigger cascading blackouts (Electric Reliability Council of Texas, 2025). This scenario is not theoretical: in July 2024, a transmission fault caused 1.5 GW of datacenters in Northern Virginia to simultaneously disconnect, requiring emergency grid management to prevent widespread outages (North American Electric Reliability Corporation, 2024).

The possibility of grid damage and blackouts from training loads has become a major impediment to building new datacenters. In some recent cases, new datacenter projects have been denied because of the instability that training can bring to the grid (Swinhoe, 2025).

This paper proposes EasyRider, a novel rack-level power supply architecture which automatically performs power smoothing as shown in Figure 1. EasyRider can be configured to satisfy any grid-imposed ramp-rate restrictions without requiring changes to existing software, models, or GPU firmware. EasyRider allows a rack to easily "ride through" a training transient without requiring circuits or systems at the datacenter or grid scale. Smoothing transients in hardware has numerous other advantages: the system can respond effectively instantaneously, can be built on physical principles that do not suffer from software bugs, provides extremely high reliability, and can be engineered to tolerate an arbitrary load up to a given maximum power magnitude.

This paper makes three research contributions:

Hardware/software architecture: EasyRider introduces a novel architecture and division of responsibilities for providing a stable power draw to the grid. Each rack-mount EasyRider power distribution unit (PDU) contains the circuitry and energy storage needed to power the rack and smooth power transients. A high-bandwidth analog control system regulates charging/discharging of the energy storage as needed to smooth transients over 30 seconds or more. A light-weight onboard software system is responsible for monitoring and managing the state of the energy storage system, maximizing its lifetime in the face of many small charge and discharge events.

Hardware system design: EasyRider  simultaneously powers a rack and removes transients through a combination of passive and regulated components. Passive components (capacitors and inductors) filter higher frequency events (≤\leq10 ms, ≥\geq100 Hz), and high-power batteries are used in closed-loop control to filter longer, low-frequency (≥\geq0.016 Hz) power fluctuations.

Software system: EasyRider uses an optimization-based control system to dynamically track a target state of charge (SoC) for the battery system. Tracking a target SoC ensures EasyRider will have sufficient stored energy to smooth future transients despite charging and discharging inefficiencies. Furthermore, it maintains battery life by avoiding deep discharges or over-charging. It also allows the system to adjust the SoC of the battery during maintenance for safe storage.

EasyRider is designed for compatibility with the future high-voltage 400​VD​C400V_{DC} datacenter regime. When compared to the cost of a GB200 rack, the per-watt capital expenditure for the power supply prototype discussed in this paper works out to less than 1.25% of the rack cost. Using EasyRider, large power swings by a GPU server or rack appear as a gradually changing power draw. When GPU power draw suddenly drops, the system charges, storing power from the grid. When GPU power suddenly increases, the system discharges, allowing time for grid power to ramp up. EasyRider can smooth millisecond-scale transients to a slow change over 30 seconds or more.

2. Background and Motivation

This section provides background on three topics that motivate EasyRider’s design. First, it describes how the grid delivers power to datacenters and why it assumes the aggregate load (power consumption) changes slowly. Second, it explains why modern large-scale training workloads break this assumption, introducing large and fast transients. Third, it goes into the power architecture of modern datacenters as well as some current and proposed approaches to protect the grid from training transients.

2.1. Grid Operating Parameters

At any given moment in time, the sum of all power sinks (loads) in the grid equals the sum of all power sources (generators). Some generators, such as solar panels and wind turbines, produce power according to the weather; others, such as gas, coal, nuclear, and hydro, can be controlled dynamically. The rate at which a generator can increase or decrease its power output is called the ramp rate (Group, 2021). Two physical properties govern the maximum ramp rate: the rate at which the generator can change its fuel consumption and the maximum acceleration/deceleration it can apply to the large physical turbines that generate the electrical power. For extremely fast generators such as gas, the maximum ramp rate is in the range of 10-20MW/min, even when the unit is designed for a few hundred MW maximum output (Group, 2021; Corporation, 2025; Abudu et al., 2021). These ramp rates have historically been sufficient because the aggregate load in the grid changes slowly.

At the same time, loads make assumptions about generators: in the United States, for example, the grid provides residential power at 120​VR​M​S120V_{RMS} and 60Hz, but this can vary, and must remain within 114-126VR​M​SV_{RMS} and 59.9–60.1Hz (Alberta Electric System Operator (AESO), 2025; Corporation, 2025). Devices attached to the grid assume this and can be damaged if power moves outside these ranges (Group, 2021).

If aggregate load changes faster than generators can adapt, the grid violates voltage and frequency ranges, damaging equipment. Power in must equal power out: if demand increases faster than the grid can adapt, then loads end up receiving less power than they need. This manifests as a sag in voltage and/or frequency. If demand decreases faster than the grid can adapt, the voltage and/or frequency spikes up. To protect against these violations, utilities and operators install reactive equipment that disconnects parts of the network before power moves outside of its safe parameters (Group, 2021). The danger and damage of large, fast swings is real: in 2023, the trip of a 1.5 GW load caused system-wide frequency deviations across Texas (Electric Reliability Council of Texas, 2025), and NERC’s analysis of a 2019 disturbance showed that a load oscillating at 0.25 Hz propagated across interconnections and damaged generators hundreds of miles away (Corporation, 2019; Buskirk, 2013).

2.2. AI/ML Training Power Dynamics

Historically, datacenters have operated within grid operating parameters: their power draw changes slowly, over minutes or hours. A given datacenter runs tens or hundreds of millions of different jobs, each of which is a tiny load; control planes such as Kubernetes (Kubernetes, 2014) or Borg (Verma et al., 2015) stagger job starts over seconds, as they load binaries, images, and supporting software.

Large-scale distributed training behaves differently. During synchronous data-parallel training, tens or hundreds of thousands of GPUs execute in lockstep: they compute gradients locally, then synchronize parameters through collective communication primitives like exchanging tensors or gradients.

This lockstep execution creates large, sudden power transients. Modern accelerators show 5:1 to 20:1 peak-to-idle ratios: an H100 drops from 700 W to 140 W during communication phases, while a B200 swings from 1000 W to 50 W (Li et al., 2024; Rouslan Dimitrov and Harry Petty and Neeraj Srivastava and Mathias Blake, 2025). When 10,000 GPUs undergo an event together, the cluster power can drop by 5–15 MW within hundreds of milliseconds (Choukse et al., 2025; Ontiveros et al., 2025). These are not rare events—they occur every training iteration (typically 1–10 Hz) and during every checkpoint, restart, or collective stall.

All digital computing equipment creates transients: a CPU, for example, can execute an energy-expensive memory load instruction then pause on a wfi (wait for interrupt) instruction. Power regulation circuits on motherboards, GPUs, and power supplies smooth out these <1<1 ms (>1>1 kHz) transients. Iteration-level training dynamics, synchronized collectives, and job-level events, however, create longer, lower frequency transients, in the range of 100 ms–10 s (0.1–10 Hz). This matters because this frequency range overlaps with bulk power system oscillation modes, where grid infrastructure has limited damping and protection equipment is most sensitive (Corporation, 2019). In some cases, new datacenter projects have been denied because of the instability that training can bring to the grid (Swinhoe, 2025).

2.3. Datacenter Power Hierarchy

Figure 2 shows how modern hyperscale data centers use multi-stage power-delivery systems that transform power from high-voltage 13.8 kV utility interfaces11 1 Utilities consider 13.8kV a “medium” voltage, with >>100kV, e.g., for long-range transmission lines being “high’ voltage. down to the 0.8-1.2 V low voltage rails on CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators. Utility power enters the datacenter and an on-site substation steps it down to medium- and low-voltage switchgear. Power is then routed through uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes), floor- or row-level power distribution units (PDUs), and branch circuits to individual racks (Barroso et al., 2013; Hamilton, 2009; Zhang et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2018; Piga et al., 2024).

Datacenter racks are built around DC power, historically at 48V (Barroso et al., 2013), to support CPU-centric racks with aggregate power draws of 30 kW. Current AI accelerator racks, however, can draw >>100 kW (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024) and the current roadmap includes 1 MW racks (e.g., OCP’s Mt. Diablo (Jason Adrian, Laurentiu Olariu, Banhu Sok, 2024)). This enormous power density—1,000 homes in a single 8 ft2 rack footprint—is driven by networking density; bringing 1,000 GPUs together so tightly in a single rack allows them to communicate with higher bandwidth and lower latency. To supply this power, datacenters are transitioning from 48V to 400V DC power (Blake et al., 2025; Walton, 2025).

2.4. Existing Approaches

A training cluster is grid-safe only if its load swings are attenuated before they reach the upstream electrical plant. The relevant dynamics span both slower events such as job transitions and checkpoints and faster content that overlaps with rack-level electrical dynamics and power-system oscillation bands. Existing mitigations address parts of this problem, but at different points in the hierarchy and with different dependencies on software, firmware, or site infrastructure (Corporation, 2019; Choukse et al., 2025; Rouslan Dimitrov and Harry Petty and Neeraj Srivastava and Mathias Blake, 2025; Kennedy, 2025). Table 1 summarizes this design space.

Software burn at the GPU. One approach is to inject secondary work, such as GEMM kernels, when GPU activity or power falls below a target (Choukse et al., 2025). This can smooth some utilization drops, but only by spending extra energy and coupling protection to the training stack. If detection or control fails, the transient is exposed upstream.

Platform-specific electrical support. NVIDIA’s GB300 NVL72 adds power-shelf capacitors together with startup power capping and ramp-down support (Rouslan Dimitrov and Harry Petty and Neeraj Srivastava and Mathias Blake, 2025). This provides electrical mitigation for short (≤\leq 60 ms) transients, but it is tied to a specific platform and does not address larger energy imbalances over longer events.

Software-coordinated rack storage. Another approach is to combine rack-level batteries that dispatch on software-triggered events along with GPU power capping like the NVIDIA GB300 (Rouslan Dimitrov and Harry Petty and Neeraj Srivastava and Mathias Blake, 2025; Choukse et al., 2025). However, this approach has two key limitations. First, conventional battery chemistries such as lithium-ion are limited by the kinetics of their electrochemical reactions, which cannot respond to transients faster than tens to hundreds of milliseconds without accelerating degradation, making them fundamentally unsuited to absorb high-frequency rack-level transients. Second, the design is not fault-tolerant: because battery discharge is triggered by software telemetry, any fault or delay in the software stack would prevent the system from responding to a transient entirely.

Site-level BESS. Site batteries buffer the aggregate load seen at the grid interconnection point (Kennedy, 2025). This helps with slower site-wide variation, but it sits above the internal row and rack distribution hierarchy. It therefore does not stop rack transients from propagating through the internal power distribution before they are absorbed at the site boundary.

Scheduling-based smoothing. Bubble-filling and high-utilization schedulers reduce some iteration-level swings by keeping GPUs more uniformly utilized (Arfeen et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). These methods are complementary, but they do not provide an electrical guarantee at the rack boundary and remain sensitive to workload structure, checkpointing, and recovery events.

3. Problem Formulation

The grid does not see individual GPUs, it only sees the aggregate power draw of a datacenter and requires that this composite signal be “well-behaved.” As discussed in Section 2.1, large-scale training violates this expectation by creating large changes in power draw that occur faster than generators and protection equipment can safely respond. Grid operators therefore impose limits on how quickly a datacenter may change its power draw over time and on how much variation is allowed at fast time scales.

To make these constraints easy to reason about, we view the datacenter power trace not just as a time series but as a sum of sinusoids at different frequencies, obtained via a Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). The magnitude of the signal at 0 Hz is its average value; low frequencies correspond to slow changes, and high frequencies to rapid ones. Intuitively, the highest significant frequency in the spectrum determines how steeply the signal can change in time.

From this perspective, training racks need a low-pass filter: a circuit and/or software stack that removes high-frequency content and passes low-frequency behavior. Low-pass filters are ubiquitous in power electronics—for example, every computer power supply uses them so that a CPU sees a stable, clean voltage even though its instantaneous load changes every cycle. Training, however, stresses filters in two ways. First, it requires smoothing down to unusually low frequencies, on the order of tens of seconds (≤0.1\leq 0.1 Hz), whereas conventional filters target millisecond scales. Second, the amount of energy involved is enormous, as smoothing a transient means temporarily storing or supplying the difference between the rack’s instantaneous and average power without exposing that swing to the grid.

The advantage of viewing training transients as frequency signals is that filters are governed by well-understood circuit theory: once sized correctly, their behavior over frequency is precise and predictable. Assuming correct implementation and no component failures, a filter will shape the power trace exactly as designed.

Suppose P⁡(t)P(t) is the normalized power draw the grid sees from a datacenter. Its frequency-domain representation describes, for each frequency ff, how much of the campus power is concentrated at that rate—exactly what grid operators care about. Let S⁡(f)S(f) denote the normalized magnitude at frequency ff, scaled so it can be interpreted as the fraction of total signal power. For example, Figure 3(b) shows S⁡(1/22​H​z)≈0.1S(1/22Hz)\approx 0.1 for a specific training trace, so ≈\approx 10% of that rack’s power use is in the 1/22 Hz frequency bin.

Grid operators generally impose two kinds of limits on P⁡(t)P(t) and S⁡(f)S(f):

Frequency content.

The first limit constrains how much variation is allowed at high frequencies. The grid operator specifies a cutoff frequency fcf_{c}; all frequencies above fcf_{c} must have magnitude at most α\alpha:

S⁡(f)≤αfor all ​f≥fc.S(f)\leq\alpha\qquad\text{for all }f\geq f_{c}.

Above fcf_{c}, only a fraction α\alpha of the campus power is permitted to participate in fast oscillations. Figure 3(b) shows this constraint: the blue curve is S⁡(f)S(f) on a log–log scale, and any portion above the horizontal line at α\alpha for f≥fcf\geq f_{c} violates the spec.

Maximum ramp rate.

The second limit bounds how quickly the datacenter power can change in time:

|d​Pd​t|≤βfor all ​t,\left|\frac{dP}{dt}\right|\leq\beta\qquad\text{for all }t,

for some ramp-rate limit β\beta expressed as a fraction of rated power per second. Steep ramps correspond to excess high-frequency content: a spectrum concentrated at fast time scales inevitably produces large changes in P⁡(t)P(t) over short intervals. Figure 3(a) illustrates a power trace that repeatedly exceeds this slope bound.

If each rack’s power-delivery system is sized so that its α\alpha, β\beta limits sum to the campus-level budget, then a hall of such racks will satisfy the same aggregate constraints. If the power-delivery system for every rack satisfies these per-rack constraints, then the datacenter as a whole will do so in aggregate. Rather than reason about every workload individually, we specify EasyRider’s behavior in terms of the frequencies it attenuates or preserves. This makes it easy to check whether a given EasyRider configuration satisfies both the frequency-content and ramp-rate limits the grid imposes. EasyRider addresses both challenges—very low effective cutoff frequencies and high energy—through its hardware/software architecture and software control system, described next.

4. EasyRider Architecture

EasyRider is a PDU system that sits between a GPU rack and the row bus, reshaping the rack’s power waveform before it reaches the rest of the datacenter power system (Figure 2). It is sized for future high-density racks with 400 VD​CV_{DC} power and an 80% idle-to-peak power swing. EasyRider smooths transients (i.e. job start-up, shutdown, checkpointing) that occur on timescales from microseconds up to tens of seconds, which are too fast for the grid to respond to but to slow for traditional GPU power supplies to handle. Its actions are invisible to upstream devices: UPSes, PDUs, and substations all see a grid-compliant, low-ramp rack load. Because it operates up to 400 VD​CV_{DC} and depends only on local sensing and actuation, EasyRider can be added to next-generation racks with power sidecars (Blake et al., 2025) or retrofitted into existing datacenters with in-rack PDUs without changes to the cluster software stack.

As illustrated in Figure 4, EasyRider comprises three physical elements plus controls and a software system, with a clean decomposition. Hardware manages power over timescales faster than the grid can respond, smoothing and removing transients. Software manages energy storage over longer timescales, to maximize system lifetime without disrupting the hardware. The hardware consists of a passive input filter that attenuates high-frequency transients, a DC-DC regulator that manages rack-side voltage and current, and a rack-scale battery bank that absorbs or injects energy during lower-frequency swings. A controller monitors battery capacity and current and issues slow corrective charge/discharge adjustments so that the battery stays within its preferred operating window while enforcing the grid-facing limits on ramp rate and frequency content.

Together, these stages present a smoothed rack load that satisfies the frequency and ramp-rate specifications from Section 3 while leaving the underlying training job unchanged. Section 5 details the filter, converter, and battery design; Section 6 describes the control loop that keeps the battery in a narrow mid-SOC band to avoid long-term drift and aging.

5. Hardware Design

This section describes EasyRider’s three hardware elements: an input filter, a DC-DC converter, and an auxiliary battery energy storage system storage system. These components work in concert to remove transients from a rack’s power draw and ensure it meets grid specifications. This decomposition handles any power signal that stays within the system’s maximum provisioned power: it requires no changes to software, can be deployed on existing racks, and will operate correctly even if the software management system fails, although multi-hour software downtimes might age the battery system slightly faster as they move outside their optimal operating range.

There are two major challenges to the hardware design: smoothing an extremely broad range of frequencies and being able to store as well as release the large amounts of energy that a rack can require at those timescales. A 1 MW rack, for example, draws the equivalent power of ≈\approx800 average U.S. homes. At such a power level, to completely smooth a 80% drop in rack power for just six seconds would require storing 4.8 MJ, which is more than what an average U.S. house draws in an hour  (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2024).

Figure 5 shows a simplified circuit schematic for the hardware system. Assuming the rack is provided with adequate energy storage capacity and a proper input filter, this design can be adapted to meet any grid specification while the rack sees immediate power availability.

Where EasyRider sits. EasyRider moves mitigation to the rack PDU, between the accelerator rack and the row bus, and splits the problem by timescale. A passive LC stage attenuates fast transients directly in the electrical path, while a local battery compensates for slower variations. This removes the transient fast path from the training stack and delayed telemetry without requiring site-level buffering. In this comparison, EasyRider is the only approach that is both rack-local and software-independent in the transient path.

5.1. Input Filter

The filter shown in Figure 5 is a second-order passive filter with a resistive damping leg. The combination of capacitor CFC_{F} and inductor LFL_{F} stabilizes the input voltage VI​NV_{IN} and input current iD​Ci_{DC} from the datacenter DC busbar over small timescales (<50 ms).

By themselves, however, LFL_{F} and CFC_{F} are not sufficient to satisfy grid specifications. They have two limitations. First, every capacitor/inductor pair has a resonant frequency, at which they can interact and enter a cycle of charging and discharging each other. The damping circuit composed of RD​aR_{Da} and LD​aL_{Da} is inactive when the rack power is steady, but it suppresses this resonance during transients. Second, because the energy density of inductors and capacitors is low, the input filter does not store very much energy—smoothing transients that last more than a few milliseconds would require a prohibitively large passive filter. It is only useful for smoothing high-frequency power fluctuations. It also filters out the high-frequency noise introduced to the system by the swtiching components in the voltage regulator and bidirectional converter.

5.2. DC-DC Converter

The DC-DC converter maintains a constant output voltage, VO​U​TV_{OUT} which powers the rack. The controls for the voltage regulator in our design are implemented fully in hardware, meaning there is no processing time delay as in a software-based system. It responds and corrects for even small errors in output voltage in less than a millisecond. The converter regulates VO​U​TV_{OUT} to within 0.7% of the rated rack voltage even if the rack power changes with ramp rates as high as ±\pm200 kW/second.

5.3. Auxiliary Energy Storage System

Because the passive filter can’t store enough energy to smooth out long transients, EasyRider uses an actively controlled energy storage system to buffer against changes in rack power over longer timescales. When the rack’s power drops, the storage system charges, absorbing the extra power from the grid. When the rack’s power rises, the storage system discharges, temporarily providing power to the rack until the grid supply can catch up. High-bandwidth sensors detect changes in rack power and automatically trigger the flow of current into or out of the storage system to make up the difference such that the value iI​N≈iD​C+iBi_{IN}\approx i_{DC}+i_{B} is stable over longer timescales. Our prototype, for example, buffers rack power fluctuations such that the DC supply takes about 30 seconds after a step change in rack power before tapering off to the new steady state. Figure 6 demonstrates the smoothing effect of the battery system during a preliminary test of the EasyRider prototype.

Traditional grid batteries are designed to provide power for hours, while EasyRider only needs a few minutes worth of capacity. In our prototype, we use high-power lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries as energy storage, due to their high power-to-capacity ratio and low cost per unit energy. Supercapacitors or a combination of different energy storage technologies could also meet EasyRider’s storage needs. The key sizing requirements and control dynamics for this system are defined in Appendix A.1.

5.4. Filter Response

The response of a filter describes how it behaves over different frequencies. EasyRider’s hardware essentially consists of two filters (the passive input filter and the controlled battery system), and its behavior is the simple multiplication of their responses. The components used in the input filter and energy storage system must be sized appropriately to comply with the grid specifications discussed in Section 3. Appendix A.1 describes how the correct sizes are derived from the rack power rating and grid specifications.

A second-order LC filter like the one pictured in Figure 5 has a cutoff frequency fff_{f}. At frequencies higher than fff_{f}, the filter attenuates rack power fluctuations by a factor of as much as 100 for every 10x increase in frequency. Our implementation of EasyRider uses a cutoff frequency ff≈4f_{f}\approx 4 Hz, and Figure 7 shows its frequency response attenuating fluctuations above this frequency. Without the controlled auxiliary energy system, a sinusoidal change in rack power with f=1f=1 Hz will not be dampened at all by the input filter, while a fluctuation at f=1000f=1000 Hz will be cut by a factor of ≈\approx 1000, as observed by the grid.

The auxiliary energy system is also a filter. Its cutoff frequency, fbf_{b}, is lower than fcf_{c}, but its system control dynamics are such that frequencies are attentuated by a factor of only 10 for every 10x in frequency above fbf_{b}.

These two filters compound. Figure 7 shows the total frequency response of the EasyRider system as the product of the input filter and auxiliary system’s responses.

6. Battery Lifetime Management

EasyRider’s hardware path handles all fast transients autonomously: the passive LC filter and controlled battery system absorb and release energy at the speed the rack demands, with no software in the loop. Because the battery charge and discharge efficiencies (ηc\eta_{c} and ηd\eta_{d} respectively) are not perfect, a slower control loop is required to manage the battery’s SoC.

Every charge–discharge cycle incurs round-trip losses on the order of 1−ηc​ηd1-\eta_{c}\eta_{d} of the energy exchanged, and these losses accumulate over hours of training into a monotonic SoC drift. This can be either upward when set-point bias dominates, or downward when resistive losses dominate. Left uncorrected, the battery eventually saturates against its upper or lower safe bound, losing the symmetric headroom it needs to smooth the next transient. Dwelling at a high SoC also accelerates idle-time aging.

The software controller’s purpose is to counteract this drift. It periodically reads the battery’s state of charge from the battery management system and issues milliamp-scale corrective currents to the DC–DC stage. Because the corrective current is orders of magnitude below the rack’s transient current, the controller cannot interfere with the hardware’s filtering even if it issues an incorrect command. If the software crashes or loses connectivity, the hardware continues to smooth transients, and the only consequence is that the battery SoC begins to drift, which can be corrected on restart with no cold-start penalty. We decompose the controller into two loops that operate on different timescales: an outer loop that selects the SoC target and an inner loop that drives the battery toward the target.

Outer Loop: A slow outer loop, updated on regime changes and refreshed every few minutes, selects the SoC target S∗S^{*} the battery should track based on reducing battery aging (Xu et al., 2023). During active training, the target is a mid-band value SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} chosen to maximize symmetric charge and discharge headroom. During prolonged idle periods, such as job completion, maintenance windows, or inter-job gaps exceeding a configurable threshold TenterT_{\mathrm{enter}}, the target drops to a lower value SidleS_{\mathrm{idle}} that reduces voltage-dependent idle-time aging (Xu et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2025). The outer loop computes this storage target from the remaining usable idle budget: the time left in the idle window minus the time needed to charge back to SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} at the maximum rate. As the idle window elapses, the budget shrinks and the target rises back toward SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} automatically; when the remaining time can no longer cover the return charge, the target reverts to SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} without operator intervention.

Inner Loop: A faster inner loop, executed every 5 s, drives the battery toward the current target by solving a small convex program over a receding horizon of HH intervals. The objective balances three concerns: tracking error (distance from S∗S^{*}), maintenance-current magnitude (to limit unnecessary cycling), and command smoothness (to prevent chatter that would result in sudden drops or jumps in current to the battery). The controller applies only the first action from each solve and re-optimizes at the next interval with a fresh SoC reading from the BMS. A narrow margin of error around the target brings the current to zero so that the battery avoids unnecessary current fluctuations near S∗S^{*}. The resulting QP is small enough to solve in under 10 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, well within the 5 s update interval. The full formulation, including the storage-target computation, the QP objective and constraints, and the normalization of tuning weights appears in Appendix B.

The key property this decomposition provides is that, given any SoC within the hardware safe bounds, the inner loop is always feasible and converges to S∗S^{*} within a few control intervals without perturbing the grid-facing power quality. The controller depends on three groups of parameters: (1) battery properties such as max charge/discharge current and round trip efficiency, (2) outer-loop policy such as the mid-band SoC and idle-time SoC, and (3) inner-loop weights such as the tracking error, maintenance-current magnitude, and command smoothness. These are all set once at deployment from the battery datasheet and the desired correction timescale, with no per-workload tuning.

7. Evaluation

We structure our evaluation around four questions: (1) can EasyRider keep training loads grid-compliant without affecting jobs, (2) how does it compare to software-based solutions, (3) is the design robust across different workloads, and (4) what are the overheads and lifetime trade-offs?

7.1. Experimental Setup

Prototype rating: To evaluate our system, we constructed a prototype of the hardware design outlined in Sections 5 and 6. This prototype, pictured in Figure 8, is rated to deliver 10kW of power to a 400 VD​CV_{DC} load.22 2 The thermal design of the prototype does not support a load current above 25 A. Because DC power is the product of current and voltage, the system cannot deliver the full 10 kW when operated at lower voltages. It is equipped with a 74Ah battery bank with a max discharge rate of 2.4C.

Workloads and traces: In our evaluation we are only concerned with training jobs that exhibit swings between peak and idle power consumption. Cluster-scale traces of frontier-model training jobs are not publicly available, therefore, we rely on an existing normalized trace of a training job that exists from Choukse et al. (Choukse et al., 2025). Further for testing software approaches and prototype evaluation, we also profile training a GPT-style 125M parameter LLM on a 2-GPU NVIDIA Titan-X decommissioned server blade from our lab.

7.2. Ramp Rate & Frequency Content Compliance without Training Changes

Benchmark specifications: As discussed in Section 3, the maximum allowable ramp rate β\beta and parameters α\alpha and fcf_{c} defining restrictions on the frequency content of the grid power trace will be set by local grid operators’ requirements. To demonstrate the smoothing effect, we designed our EasyRider prototype under the assumption that the datacenter is allowed to ramp at a maximum β=0.1\beta=0.1 (10% of rated power per second) and that the grid imposes a limit S⁡(f)<α=10−4S(f)<\alpha=10^{-4} on the normalized magnitude of frequencies ff above fc=2​Hzf_{c}=2~\text{Hz}. This spec is in line with the issues described by previous work (Choukse et al., 2025; Ontiveros et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024) and addresses the band of frequecies from 0.1-10 Hz that can damage generators and turbines as noted by NERC (Corporation, 2019; Group, 2021; Corporation, 2025).

Ramp rate compliance: Figure 9(a) shows the result of using our EasyRider prototype to deliver power to a DC load following the normalized training power trace from (Choukse et al., 2025). While the rack power trace exhibits sharp power swings at each communication event and an abrupt drop at job termination, the EasyRider-conditioned trace transitions much more gradually and exhibits a lower peak power draw. Figure 9(b) shows the ramp rate across the same time period, demonstrating that EasyRider successfully smooths the rack power trace to ensure that the ramp rate never exceeds 10% of the rack’s rated power per second.

This behavior is independent of the training job’s power profile, therefore complying with the grid ramp-rate specification without modifying the workload. This decouples grid compliance from job scheduling, as any training workload can run unmodified, and EasyRider will ensure that its worst-case ramp rate never exceeds β\beta, even across start-up and shut-down phases. Importantly, the guarantee composes across racks and rows—because each EasyRider-equipped rack presents a power waveform with ∣d​P/d​t∣≤β\mid dP/dt\mid\leq\beta, the aggregate datacenter ramp rate is likewise constrained.33 3 Appendix D provides additional explanation on smoothing effects at a cluster scale. This allows operators to reason about campus-wide limits in terms of per-rack design rather than per-job coordination.

Frequency content compliance: Figure 10 shows the rack and EasyRider power traces from Figure 9(a) broken into their respective frequency components. The combined effect of the input filter and battery system is enough to shift the entire EasyRider power spectrum out of restricted zone.

This frequency response shaping has two practical implications. First, because EasyRider implements a fixed transfer function (Figure 7) at the rack-to-power-distribution connection, any training job whose raw power spectrum falls at or below the grey curve will, after conditioning, satisfy the same grid constraint without changing the model, scheduler, or GPU firmware. This means that operators can freely vary workloads as long as they stay within the rack’s rated power envelope. As with ramp rate compliance, the guarantee composes across racks and rows: each EasyRider-equipped rack enforces the same per-rack bound on S𝑔𝑟𝑖𝑑​(f)S_{\mathit{grid}}(f), so a hall of racks behaves like a collection of “tamed” loads that can be integrated under a campus-level interconnection agreement. In effect, EasyRider turns arbitrary high-frequency power fluctuations from training into a waveform whose worst-case harmonic content is known and bounded by design.

7.3. Energy Efficiency Against Software Burn-Based Solutions

Other approaches to enforcing ramp-rate limits, as discussed in Section 2.4, either rely on cluster-wide coordination or use proprietary hardware that we cannot reproduce. The most directly comparable, software-only mechanism is to inject “burn” kernels that artificially raise GPU utilization to a target power level. We therefore compare EasyRider to a software burn-based solution on our decommissioned 2-GPU Titan X blade.

To implement the software burn, we profile GEMM kernels to derive a mapping between duty cycle and GPU power, then use this mapping to schedule additional matrix multiplications that maintain or ramp to a desired power setpoint. Full details of this implementation appear in Appendix C.1. Figure 11 shows the resulting normalized power traces for the raw Titan X workload, EasyRider, and software burn. We delay the start of the Titan X trace by approximately 41 s to account for the warm-up period required by software burn, and normalize all traces to the Titan X blade’s TDP.

While observing Figure 11, we notice that EasyRider remains at a lower power level than software burn. The software burn-based solution succeeds in smoothing the power trace within the required ramp-rate envelope, but only by paying for an extended startup phase and a higher steady-state power level. Taking the integral of the power trace, we find that software burn consumes 19% more total energy than the combined rack+EasyRider configuration. As an added benefit, EasyRider does not require any additional warm-up period or changes to the training code. While EasyRider does incur some losses in its battery and power electronics, these manifest as a small additional energy sink over weeks of training, whereas software burns waste energy throughout every second of the job.

7.4. Energy Storage Stability and Lifetime

As discussed in Section 6, over hours of training, our system produces a monotonic SoC drift. Our software controller exists to counteract this drift without interfering with the hardware’s filtering.

Figure 12 demonstrates this mechanism in practice. After a few hours of operation without software control, our system drifts to approximately 62% SoC. As soon as we begin this experiment, our software controller allows the inner-loop QP (Appendix B) to issue corrective currents while the rack runs the training trace. The controller updates every 5 s, reads the current SoC from the BMS, and solves for a milliamp-scale discharge current that drives the battery toward S∗S^{*}. The “with software” trace converges to SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} within approximately 20 minutes. The “without software” trace, shows the SoC if it were to receive no corrective signal, and how it would drift in the opposite direction as the hardware path’s set-point bias pushes the SoC toward the upper safe bound.

Two properties are visible in the figure. First, the corrective current is small and changes slowly relative to the rack’s transient currents, confirming that the controller does not disturb our existing hardware filtering. Second, convergence is monotonic, as once the SoC enters the deadband |S−S∗|≤ε|S-S^{*}|\leq\varepsilon, the controller damps the current so that the battery holds position.

This experiment validates the inner loop in isolation. The outer loop’s storage-mode policy, which lowers S∗S^{*} during prolonged idle intervals to reduce calendar aging, follows the same corrective mechanism with a different target and therefore does not require separate validation. The practical implication is that the software stack adds no per-workload tuning, since SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}}, ε\varepsilon, and the QP weights are set once from the battery datasheet and the desired correction timescale, and the controller keeps the battery in its optimal operating band across arbitrary training traces.

8. Discussion

Incremental deployment across rows and halls. A key advantage of EasyRider is that it sits between each rack and the upstream power distribution. While some hyperscalers already use in-rack UPSes or other alternatives to Figure 2, EasyRider can be dropped in incrementally across rows and halls without substation or mid-voltage retrofits. Because racks and pods arrive in a staggered fashion (Baxi et al., 2025), this enables ad hoc, per-rack installations that still maintain campus ramp-rate and spectral limits.

Fault tolerance. EasyRider’s hardware continues to function safely even if its software controller is offline. As long as the battery bank is within a reasonable state of charge, the system will still smooth the rack power trace and keep ramp rates within spec. When software is available, the controller simply re-optimizes assuming a constant rack power setpoint, so there is no cold-start penalty when a job begins or when the controller restarts.

Minimal and isolated software. The software stack is deliberately small and decoupled from training jobs. Its only roles are to measure battery state-of-charge and current and to issue slow, corrective current adjustments that keep the battery in a healthy SoC and voltage range. In our prototype, a Raspberry Pi polls the battery management system over Modbus and gates balancing current to the battery pack; this implementation is identical across racks and does not interact with model code, frameworks, or schedulers, simplifying replication and scaling.

Cost and deployment complexity. Our 10 kW prototype cost approximately $3,500 to build. A large fraction of this bill of materials comes from the 74 Ah battery pack, which is intentionally oversized relative to the requirements derived in Appendix A.1. Costs are higher than a production design because we rely on individually purchased, commodity modules rather than battery pooling and integrated power stages. However, in our current deployment we achieve $0.35/W which for a GB200 rack is approximately $66,000 per rack. At an estimated rack cost of $3.7M, this is less than 1.25% of the rack cost. In a deployment setting, the primary additional constraint is physical as well. The filter and converter must fit within the rack or immediately adjacent to it to preserve the electrical behavior characterized in this paper which will drive mechanical and thermal co-design but not require changes to upstream substations.

9. Related Work

Characterization of AI Training Power Dynamics. Large swings in compute load have been documented in HPC systems for over a decade (Bates et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2021; Patki et al., 2025; Stewart et al., 2019). This literature studies how large compute clusters interact with the grid, quantifies problematic ramp rates and oscillations, and considers scheduler-level mitigation. Our setting is different, since recent work has shown that large AI training jobs create tightly synchronized, multi-megawatt swings with distinct temporal structure (Li and Li, 2025; Li et al., 2024; Ontiveros et al., 2025). EasyRider builds on that observation, but targets mitigating these transient risks, not just characterizing the loads.

Datacenter Power Management. Prior datacenter power-management systems treat power as a shared resource to allocate, cap, or oversubscribe through cluster-level control (Wu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Ellsworth et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2018; Piga et al., 2024; Kumbhare et al., 2021). Similar work uses batteries and UPSes for peak shaving and other site-level services over longer timescales (Zheng et al., 2015; Shao et al., 2020; Bianchini et al., 2024). These systems determine when, where, and how much power workloads may consume. EasyRider addresses a different layer, as it conditions the rack’s electrical load before that load reaches the upstream power hiearchy, and is therefore complementary to existing control-plane mechanisms.

AI/ML Training Power Management. Recent work on AI training power and energy management reduces energy consumption by changing training behavior through profiling, scheduling, DVFS, or power capping (Chung et al., 2024; You et al., 2023; Koszczal et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2023). The goal in this literature is to improve job-level energy efficiency or fit workloads within cluster power budgets. EasyRider does not modify the training job; instead, it leaves the workload unchanged and reshapes the resulting power draw in the rack PDU.

Industry characterization and proposals. Existing industry proposals mitigate training transients at different points in the stack: some shape computation through burn or power capping (Ontiveros et al., 2025; Rouslan Dimitrov and Harry Petty and Neeraj Srivastava and Mathias Blake, 2025), while others buffer power at the platform or site boundary (Kennedy, 2025). Related analyses of AI load dynamics have also clarified the grid-side risk created by synchronized training loads (Li et al., 2024; Ontiveros et al., 2025). Other proposals consider rack-level storage coordinated with software control (Choukse et al., 2025). Across these efforts, the hardware and software roles in transient mitigation remain only loosely separated. EasyRider is able to manage transients in hardware which is fast and path independent from the software stack.

10. Conclusion

In this paper we presented EasyRider, a per-rack power system that conditions training power before it reaches upstream distribution and the grid. EasyRider combines a passive filter, an actively controlled rack-scale battery, and a DC regulator to power the rack and smooth transients as long as tens of seconds and enforce grid-facing limits on ramp rate and frequency content without modifying the training stack. A lightweight optimization controller monitors and maintains battery health over time. Using a 10 kW prototype on normalized cluster traces and real GPU training workloads, we show that EasyRider meets these grid constraints while incurring substantially lower energy and runtime overheads than software burn–based approaches. Because it sits entirely behind the rack PDU and relies only on local sensing and control, EasyRider can be incrementally deployed across existing and future high-voltage DC racks, providing a practical path to grid-safe AI clusters as model and rack power continue to scale.

Appendix A Hardware Components: Values and Sizing

A.1. Component Sizing

Energy storage capacity: Suppose we are using EasyRider to ride through the power transients of a rack with a themal design power (TDP) of PR​A​T​E​DP_{RATED}. The design depends on an adequately sized energy storage system, whether using batteries, supercapacitors, or any other storage mechanism. The DC-DC regulator stage maintains the voltage at the input of the rack at a constant VO​U​T=VD​CV_{OUT}=V_{DC}, so power diverted to the auxiliary energy storage branch at any given time (t)(t) is

(1) PB​(t)=VD​C⋅iB​(t)P_{B}(t)=V_{DC}\cdot i_{B}(t)

EasyRider ‘s energy storage system is controlled in our design such that the current iBi_{B} is fixed by the differential equation

(2) dd​t​iB+β⋅iB+dd​t​iR=0\frac{d}{dt}i_{B}+\beta\cdot i_{B}+\frac{d}{dt}i_{R}=0

which ensures that the maximum ramp rate that the EasyRider system imposes on the grid can never exceed β⋅PR​A​T​E​D\beta\cdot P_{RATED}, even if the rack were to turn off altogether. (β\beta is chosen to meet the system ramp rate restriction as shown in Figure 3(a), discussed in Section 3.)

If we assume that at time t=0t=0, iRi_{R} has been constant at some current I1I_{1} for some time, and then over a period of some time it transitions to some current I2I_{2} and holds steady, the net energy (in joules) stored in the during the transient under ideal conditions is

(3) ΔEB=VD​C∫0∞iBdt=−VD​Cβ∫0∞dd​t(iR+iB)dt\Delta E_{B}=V_{DC}\int_{0}^{\infty}i_{B}dt=-\frac{V_{DC}}{\beta}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d}{dt}(i_{R}+i_{B})dt

From equation 2 we know that the battery current decays to zero when the rack current is constant. Then

(4) Δ​EB=−VD​Cβ​[iR​(t)+iB​(t)]t=0t=∞=VD​Cβ​(I1−I2)\Delta E_{B}=-\frac{V_{DC}}{\beta}[i_{R}(t)+i_{B}(t)]_{t=0}^{t=\infty}=\frac{V_{DC}}{\beta}(I_{1}-I_{2})

The maximum change in rack power as a proportion of total TDP is

(5) ϵ=PR​A​T​E​D−PM​I​NPR​A​T​E​D\epsilon=\frac{P_{RATED}-P_{MIN}}{P_{RATED}}

where PM​I​NP_{MIN} is the minimum (≥0\geq 0) rack power in watts. Because the energy storage system won’t ever charge unless the rack power has generally decreased, and the system won’t ever discharge unless the rack power has generally increased, the maximum magnitude of Δ​EB\Delta E_{B} in equation 4 occurs for I1=PR​A​T​E​DVD​CI_{1}=\frac{P_{RATED}}{V_{DC}}, I2=PM​I​NVD​CI_{2}=\frac{P_{MIN}}{V_{DC}}, the maximum and minimum possible rack currents, repectively:

(6) |Δ​EB|≤Δ​EB|I1=PR​A​T​E​DVD​C,I2=PM​I​NVD​C\left|\Delta E_{B}\right|\leq\Delta\left.E_{B}\right|_{I_{1}=\frac{P_{RATED}}{V_{DC}},I_{2}=\frac{P_{MIN}}{V_{DC}}}

Therefore we can conclude that the net energy stored during any rack power trace is bounded by

(7) Δ​EB≤ϵβ​PR​A​T​E​D\Delta E_{B}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\beta}P_{RATED}

Finally, if you are restricted to using only some proportion γ\gamma of the total capacity of the energy storage mechanism—as in the case of batteries, which may need to be kept in a 40-60% state of charge to prevent rapid aging—the minimum viable storage capacity EBE_{B} in joules is

(8) EB≥ϵγ​β​PR​A​T​E​DE_{B}\geq\frac{\epsilon}{\gamma\beta}P_{RATED}

Energy storage power rating: The energy storage system must also be capable of sourcing or sinking power at a sufficient rate to maintain compliance with grid ramp rate specifications. From equation 2 we can see that the maximum power that the energy storage system must be capable of sourcing or sinking occurs when the rack power changes instantaneously from its maximum to minimum value or vice versa. It follows that the energy storage system needs to be rated to charge or discharge at a power level of at least

(9) PB≥ϵ​PR​A​T​E​DP_{B}\geq\epsilon P_{RATED}

where ϵ\epsilon is as defined in equation 5.

Input filter components: The input filter’s primary function is to attenuate high-frequency power fluctuations in order to comply with the frequency content specification laid out in Section 3. The control dynamics of the energy storage system shown in equation 2 already ensure that power fluctuations with harmonic content above fb=β2​πf_{b}=\frac{\beta}{2\pi} Hz are attenuated by a factor of 10 for every 10x increase in frequency. Because this may not be adequate on its own, the input filter provides additional attenuation of higher-frequency power fluctuations.

A second-order LC filter like the one shown in Figure 5 attenuates rack power fluctuations by a factor of as much as 100 for every 10x increase in frequency above its cutoff frequency fff_{f}. Depending on the characteristics of the rack power profile, the cutoff frequency is chosen such that the grid power harmonic content is acceptable under the grid specifications. Because fff_{f} is a function of the filter component values, the inductance LL and capacitance CC of the filter should be chosen to achieve the desired cutoff frequency using the standard formula for a second-order LC filter:

(10) ff=12​π​L​Cf_{f}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}

The total system frequency response is shown in Figure 7.

Appendix B Controller Formulation

This appendix states the outer- and inner-loop optimization problems solved by EasyRider’s software controller (Section 6).

B.1. Outer Loop: SoC Target Selection

The outer loop selects a target S∗S^{*} from two modes:

Active mode (S∗=SmidS^{*}=S_{\mathrm{mid}}).

During training, the target is fixed at SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} to preserve symmetric headroom.

Storage mode.

When the predicted idle interval exceeds TenterT_{\mathrm{enter}} and the reachable SoC reduction exceeds a minimum useful shift Δ​Smin\Delta S_{\mathrm{min}}, the target drops to

(11) Sstorage∗=max⁡(Sidle,Smid−Δ​Smax,Ssafe,min),S^{*}_{\mathrm{storage}}=\max\!\bigl(S_{\mathrm{idle}},\;S_{\mathrm{mid}}-\Delta S_{\max},\;S_{\mathrm{safe,min}}\bigr),

where Δ​Smax=imax​max⁡(0,Tremain−Tready​(Sidle))/(ηd​Qmax)\Delta S_{\max}=i^{\max}\,\max(0,\,T_{\mathrm{remain}}-T_{\mathrm{ready}}(S_{\mathrm{idle}}))\;/\;(\eta_{d}\,Q_{\max}) and Tready​(S)=(Smid−S)​Qmax/(ηc​imax)T_{\mathrm{ready}}(S)=(S_{\mathrm{mid}}-S)\,Q_{\max}/(\eta_{c}\,i^{\max}) is the time required to charge from SS back to SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}}. Because TremainT_{\mathrm{remain}} decreases as the idle window elapses, Sstorage∗S^{*}_{\mathrm{storage}} rises toward SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}} automatically. When Tremain<Tready​(Scurrent)T_{\mathrm{remain}}<T_{\mathrm{ready}}(S_{\mathrm{current}}), the target reverts to SmidS_{\mathrm{mid}}. In our prototype, Tenter=4T_{\mathrm{enter}}=4 h and Δ​Smin=0.02\Delta S_{\mathrm{min}}=0.02.

B.2. Inner Loop: Receding-Horizon QP

Let ℐ=(i0,…,iH−1)\mathcal{I}=(i_{0},\dots,i_{H-1}) be the corrective currents over HH intervals of length Δ​t\Delta t, and let 𝒮=(S0,…,SH)\mathcal{S}=(S_{0},\dots,S_{H}) be the predicted SoC trajectory initialized at the measured value S^t\hat{S}_{t}. Define normalized variables

(12) uk=ikimax,ek=Sk−S∗Δ​Sref,u_{k}=\frac{i_{k}}{i^{\max}},\qquad e_{k}=\frac{S_{k}-S^{*}}{\Delta S_{\mathrm{ref}}},

where Δ​Sref=Smid−Sidle\Delta S_{\mathrm{ref}}=S_{\mathrm{mid}}-S_{\mathrm{idle}}.

The inner loop solves

(13) minℐ\displaystyle\min_{\mathcal{I}}\;\; ∑k=0H−1[ek+12+λI​uk2+λΔ​(uk−uk−1)2]+λT​eH2\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\!\Bigl[e_{k+1}^{2}+\lambda_{I}\,u_{k}^{2}+\lambda_{\Delta}\,(u_{k}-u_{k-1})^{2}\Bigr]+\lambda_{T}\,e_{H}^{2}
(14) s.t.   Sk+1=Sk+Δ​tQmax​(ηc​[ik]+−ηd−1​[−ik]+),\displaystyle S_{k+1}=S_{k}+\frac{\Delta t}{Q_{\max}}\bigl(\eta_{c}\,[i_{k}]^{+}-\eta_{d}^{-1}\,[-i_{k}]^{+}\bigr),
(15) S0=S^t,\displaystyle S_{0}=\hat{S}_{t},
(16) Ssafe,min≤Sk≤Ssafe,max,\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{safe,min}}\leq S_{k}\leq S_{\mathrm{safe,max}},

where u−1u_{-1} is the previously applied normalized current and [x]+=max⁡(x,0)[x]^{+}=\max(x,0). The controller applies only i0i_{0} and re-solves at the next interval. If |S^t−S∗|≤ε|\hat{S}_{t}-S^{*}|\leq\varepsilon, it sets the current to zero.

The three ratios λI\lambda_{I}, λΔ\lambda_{\Delta}, λT\lambda_{T} trade off tracking speed against current magnitude and command smoothness. We set them from two design targets: the desired correction timescale for a representative SoC deviation, and the desired smoothness of the maintenance-current trajectory. The problem is a small convex QP, feasible whenever S^t\hat{S}_{t} lies within hardware safe bounds.

Appendix C Software Components

C.1. GPU Burn Algorithm for Baseline

Calibration. We first calibrate a tiny matrix–multiply kernel to learn a linear mapping between its duty cycle and GPU power, and then invert this mapping so we can interpolate for a target power and get back a duty cycle that achieves it. Here the duty cycle d∈[0,1]d\in[0,1] is the fraction of each fixed control window TwinT_{\text{win}} that the GPU spends actively running the GEMM kernel (for time d⋅Twind\cdot T_{\text{win}}) versus sleeping (for time (1−d)⋅Twin(1-d)\cdot T_{\text{win}}), which smoothly scales the average power between idle (d≈0d\approx 0) and near-TDP (d≈1d\approx 1). Concretely, we run two small calibration tools on a single Titan X: one sweeps over matrix sizes NN and duty cycles d∈[0,1]d\in[0,1] using a duty-cycled GEMM loop in fixed windows and logs the resulting average GPU power to CSV, and the other uses the same GEMM burner to sweep only over dd for a fixed NN. We then fit a simple linear model P⁡(d)≈a​d+bP(d)\approx ad+b on the stable regime of the sweep and invert it to obtain d⁡(P)d(P) for our runtime ramps and checkpoint compensation.

Integration in Training Loop. In Algorithm 2 we show how we implement our GEMM burns during training. During warmup, before the first training step, we repeatedly run the kernel on both GPUs, gradually increasing the target power from a low “warmup” level to the normal training power over a fixed time window (e.g., 30 s). This creates a smooth ramp from idle to full load instead of a step change. The training loop is otherwise standard, except at each checkpoint. Since our GPUs are connected by NVLink, there is no need to communicate over a network and therefore the only dips we see are from the checkpointing itself. When rank 0 saves a checkpoint and its power drops, the other GPUs temporarily run the burn kernel at a higher target power chosen so that the sum of GPU power stays close to the normal training level. All ranks synchronize at a barrier before resuming training. After the last step, we run a symmetric cooldown: both GPUs gradually reduce their target power from the training level down to a lower “cool” level using the same burn kernel, again over a fixed time window. This produces a smooth ramp down to near-idle instead of a sudden drop.

Gloo and NCCL Barriers. To make sure we can run checkpoint burn compensation without sacrificing training performance, we use a dual process group approach. We initialize two separate PyTorch distributed process groups: a primary NCCL group for all training communication (gradient synchronization, model updates), and a secondary Gloo group exclusively for checkpoint barriers. NCCL barriers enqueue operations on the CUDA stream, which blocks subsequent GPU kernels and prevents our GEMM burn from executing concurrently, something that Gloo barriers which use CPU-based synchronization primitives do not do. By routing only checkpoint synchronization through the Gloo group while maintaining NCCL for all training operations, we can achieve full NCCL training performance while allowing other GPUs to run compensation burns concurrently during checkpointing.

Appendix D Explanation of Smoothing at Scale

The smoothing effect of EasyRider at the campus-wide scale follows from the fact that the total datacenter power use is a sum of all the individual system demands. For a cluster spread across N racks, we can break down the total cluster IT load PI​T​(t)P_{IT}(t) into the sum of the instantaneous power demands of each rack:

(18) PI​T​(t)=∑i=1NPi​(t)P_{IT}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_{i}(t)

In syncronous training, because all the individual power traces across a cluster are essentially the same,

(19) PI​T​(t)=N⋅Pi​(t)P_{IT}(t)=N\cdot P_{i}(t)

and furthermore because the DFT is a linear function, it also allows scaling by a linear multiplier—the power spectrum for the cluster is proportional to the power spectrum of the individual racks operating in synchrony:

(20) SI​T​(f)=N⋅Si​(f)S_{IT}(f)=N\cdot S_{i}(f)

Although the prototype demonstrated in this paper is only rated for 10 kW as a proof of concept and does not singlehandedly handle enough power to smooth grid-scale fluctuations, the scaling relations in equations 19 and 20 assert that the normalized results we show in the paper for a single rack would look identical at the cluster scale, were every rack equipped with an EasyRider power supply.

Figure 13 shows the expected smoothing behavior on a 40 MW training cluster were every rack equipped with an individual EasyRider power supply. Because EasyRider smooths each rack’s power, the aggregate cluster power PI​TP_{IT} is also smoothed.
